glossary.definition: The model processes input prompt tokens to build attention state before generating the first output token.
The autoregressive phase generates output tokens one at a time while reusing the accumulated key/value cache.
Time to first token, including queue wait and prompt prefill before the first generated token is available.
Stored attention keys and values for previous tokens, reducing recomputation but consuming memory proportional to layers, heads, sequence length and precision.
A serving scheduler that dynamically admits and retires sequences so accelerator work remains utilized as requests arrive and finish.
A memory-management approach that stores KV blocks in pages to reduce fragmentation and support flexible sequence allocation.
Representing model weights or KV values with fewer bits to reduce memory/bandwidth at a possible quality or stability cost.
A draft model proposes multiple tokens and a target model verifies them, potentially increasing decode throughput when acceptance is high.
A gate that accepts, queues or rejects work based on capacity, memory, deadline and service-level constraints.
A long or resource-heavy request delays later requests even when those later requests could otherwise make progress.

explanation.problem: A model server can fail even when the model fits in memory: concurrent long prompts exhaust KV cache, queues grow faster than decode capacity, p95 latency breaches SLOs, and retries amplify overload. Optimizing only tokens per second can make TTFT or fairness worse. Capacity engineering requires explicit memory estimates, workload distributions, bounded admission and measured trade-offs.
explanation.plainLanguage:
Split inference into two phases. During prefill, the model processes the prompt and builds attention state; this phase often benefits from parallel compute. During decode, output tokens are generated autoregressively and depend on previous tokens, so memory bandwidth and KV-cache access matter. TTFT includes queue wait plus prefill. Inter-token latency and output throughput describe the decode phase. Measure both rather than reporting one average latency.

The KV cache stores keys and values for every active sequence. A simplified estimate is: 2 × layers × KV heads × head dimension × bytes per value × sequence tokens × concurrent sequences. For 32 layers, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128 and FP16 values (2 bytes), each token uses 128 KiB. A 4,096-token sequence uses about 512 MiB before allocator fragmentation, weights, activations, runtime overhead and other buffers. Grouped-query attention, tensor parallelism, cache layout and serving engine change the real number.

Batching improves utilization but creates scheduling trade-offs. Static batches wait for the slowest sequence; continuous batching admits and retires sequences dynamically. A scheduler needs limits for batch size, queue depth, context length, per-tenant fairness, deadlines and KV memory. When capacity is exceeded, reject or shed load with a clear reason instead of allowing unbounded memory and latency growth. Retries must be bounded and coordinated to avoid retry storms.

Prefix caching can avoid repeated prefill for shared prompt prefixes, but the cache key must include tenant/security scope and prompt/model version. A cross-tenant cache hit can leak information or reuse an unauthorized prefix. Paged attention reduces fragmentation by managing KV blocks, but does not remove the memory requirement.

Quantization reduces weight or KV storage and may improve bandwidth, but can affect quality and numerical stability. Speculative decoding uses a draft model to propose tokens and a target model to verify them; speedup depends on acceptance rate and verification overhead. These are measured trade-offs, not universal wins.

Run capacity sweeps over prompt/output lengths, concurrency, arrival rate, batch size, cache hit rate and precision. Report TTFT, inter-token latency, p50/p95, throughput, queue wait, rejected requests, KV memory and quality deltas. Simulators teach the accounting and failure modes; production capacity must be measured on the actual model, hardware, engine, kernel and workload.

Capacity planning uses Little's Law: average in-flight requests L = arrival rate λ × average time W. It is an average relationship for a stable system, not a peak concurrency limit. Combine it with measured arrival bursts, p95 latency, prompt/output distributions and per-tenant fairness. A round-robin scheduler gives each active tenant a turn; a paged allocator tracks reservations and must release pages after completion or cancellation. Versioned prefix cache keys include tenant, model, prompt and policy so cached context cannot cross security or release boundaries.
explanation.mentalModel: Request arrival → admission and tenant fairness → queue/batch scheduler → KV memory reservation → prefill/TTFT → decode loop → optional prefix/speculative optimizations → latency, throughput, memory and quality telemetry.
limitations: The local simulator uses synthetic throughput curves and does not model real GPU kernels, bandwidth, interconnect or hardware scheduling.
The KV formula is a simplified estimate; real attention layouts, GQA/MQA, tensor parallelism, cache blocks and allocator overhead vary.
The speculative decoding multiplier is illustrative and does not predict a particular draft/target model pair.
The quantization quality penalty is a teaching assumption, not a measured benchmark.
The prefix cache models tenant key isolation but not distributed cache eviction, encryption or concurrency races.
The simulator's queue and batch scheduler is deterministic and simplified; production continuous batching requires a real serving engine.
A memory estimate that fits KV cache alone does not prove the model, weights, activations and runtime fit on a device.
explanation.everydayAnalogy: A restaurant kitchen has a prep phase and a cooking phase. More chefs can prepare many orders in parallel, but each active table still occupies space and each dish needs time at the stove. The manager controls reservations, table capacity and queue length. Serving systems do the same with prompt prefill, decode, KV memory and admission control.
explanation.mathMadeSimple: For a decoder with L=32 layers, Hkv=8 key/value heads, D=128 dimensions per head, 2 bytes per value and S=4,096 tokens: KV bytes = 2×L×Hkv×D×2×S = 536,870,912 bytes = 512 MiB for one sequence. Two concurrent sequences need about 1 GiB before other memory overhead. Little's Law example: 2 requests/second × 0.5 seconds average time = 1 request in flight on average. Burst and tail-latency headroom are still required.
explanation.productionImpact: Measure TTFT and inter-token latency separately; estimate and reserve KV memory before admission; use continuous batching and bounded queues; isolate prefix caches by tenant and version; tune quantization/speculative decoding on quality-aware benchmarks; enforce deadlines, fairness and load shedding; and validate every estimate on the actual serving engine and hardware.

useCase.scenario: An enterprise AI service receives mixed workloads: short customer questions, long document analysis and bursts from multiple tenants. The platform must keep p95 latency within target, prevent KV exhaustion, share prefix cache safely, and reject excess load predictably.

trustBoundaries: Tenant identity and cache scope come from verified request context.
Prompt and output lengths are validated before reservation.
Model/runtime throughput assumptions are configuration, not observed hardware facts.
A cache key includes tenant and model/prompt version.
Admission and budget enforcement happen before expensive execution.
failurePaths: KV cache exceeds budget: reject or defer before execution; never allocate unbounded state.
Queue overload: shed load and return retry guidance rather than growing memory without limit.
Head-of-line blocking: inspect batch composition, priority and per-tenant fairness.
Prefix cache collision: partition keys by tenant and model/prompt version.
Quantization degrades quality: compare quality and memory/latency on a held-out evaluation set.
Speculative acceptance falls: disable the draft path when verification overhead exceeds benefit.
Deadline miss: separate queue wait, prefill and decode contributions.
Tenant starvation: rotate non-empty tenant queues fairly and enforce per-tenant active caps.
KV allocation leak after cancellation: release the exact request allocation and verify free-page count returns to baseline.

failures.name: KV-cache exhaustion
failures.symptom: A model server runs out of memory when long sequences arrive concurrently.
failures.rootCause: Capacity planning ignores active sequence length, KV heads, precision or concurrency.
failures.recovery: Estimate KV cache before admission, reserve headroom and shed load when budget is exceeded.
failures.regressionTest: Create two 4,096-token sequences under a 512 MiB budget and assert the batch is rejected.

failures.name: Queue overload and retry storm
failures.symptom: Queue depth and p95 latency grow continuously during bursts.
failures.rootCause: Unbounded queue, unlimited retries or no admission control.
failures.recovery: Bound queue and retries, apply load shedding and return explicit retry guidance.
failures.regressionTest: Exceed max_queue and assert excess requests are rejected with a stable reason.

failures.name: Head-of-line blocking
failures.symptom: Short requests wait behind a very long prompt or generation.
failures.rootCause: Static batching or poor scheduling/fairness policy.
failures.recovery: Measure per-request wait, use continuous batching or workload-aware scheduling and tenant fairness.
failures.regressionTest: Vary arrival and output lengths; assert queue wait is visible and batch composition is deterministic.

failures.name: Prefix cache tenant collision
failures.symptom: A tenant receives a cache hit for another tenant's prompt prefix.
failures.rootCause: Cache key omits tenant, model or prompt version.
failures.recovery: Partition cache keys by tenant and model/prompt revision.
failures.regressionTest: Reuse a prefix key across two tenants and assert only the original tenant hits.

failures.name: Quantization quality regression
failures.symptom: Memory falls but output quality or numerical stability drops.
failures.rootCause: Precision changed without evaluating model/task quality.
failures.recovery: Benchmark precision variants against held-out quality and stability guardrails.
failures.regressionTest: Assert lower-bit modes expose a quality penalty alongside memory savings.

failures.name: Speculative decode acceptance collapse
failures.symptom: Draft model adds overhead without improving throughput.
failures.rootCause: Acceptance rate is low or target verification cost dominates.
failures.recovery: Measure accepted tokens and disable speculative path when it loses.
failures.regressionTest: Set acceptance to zero and assert no modeled throughput gain.

failures.name: Deadline miss
failures.symptom: A request exceeds its latency objective even though the model remains available.
failures.rootCause: Queue wait, prefill and decode are not budgeted separately.
failures.recovery: Track each latency component, reserve capacity and reject work that cannot meet deadlines.
failures.regressionTest: Use a slow synthetic profile and assert deadline_missed is true.

failures.name: Tenant starvation
failures.symptom: A high-volume tenant occupies every active batch while smaller tenants wait.
failures.rootCause: Scheduler uses global FIFO or priority without per-tenant rotation and concurrency limits.
failures.recovery: Use bounded round-robin scheduling and per-tenant active caps.
failures.regressionTest: Submit several requests from tenant A plus one each from B/C; verify B/C enter the first fair batch.

failures.name: KV page leak after cancellation
failures.symptom: Free KV pages do not return after a request is canceled or completed.
failures.rootCause: Request lifecycle does not release the matching allocation.
failures.recovery: Track allocations by request ID and release exactly once on every terminal path.
failures.regressionTest: Allocate, cancel/release and assert free page count returns to its original value.

codeWalkthrough.explanation: This simplified formula estimates K and V storage for each layer, KV head, dimension and cached token. Multiply by concurrency for independent active sequences.
Queue wait and prefill determine TTFT; decode contributes generation time after the first token. Keep these components separate.
Reserve memory before admitting a batch. Predictable rejection is safer than unbounded allocation and cascading OOM.
Prefix caching is a data-isolation boundary. A shared string prefix must not create cross-tenant or cross-model reuse.
Speculative decoding speedup depends on accepted draft tokens and verification overhead; benchmark the actual target/draft pair.
Little's Law estimates average in-flight work in a stable system. It does not replace burst, p95 or deadline testing.
Round-robin scheduling rotates non-empty tenant queues so one busy tenant cannot monopolize each batch.
Fixed-size KV pages are tracked per request and must be released on completion or cancellation to avoid capacity leaks.
